# What is an exchange?

*You'll need nothing before this chapter. It defines the order book, orders, fills, the position limit and profit,
which every later chapter uses.*

## The story

The Varde rehearsal's first upload (chapter 1) scored €110.21 on its first public session. The portal showed only
totals and a file of fills, and the session rebuilt the rest by hand; the portal's own scoring code, run on the same
bot, shows where the number comes from. It is two large numbers that nearly cancel
[(`data/sessions.csv`, from the rehearsal portal's own scoring)]{.src}:

- **cash: −€2,814.63.** Over the session the bot spent more on buying than it received from selling, fees included.
- **the position, valued: +€2,924.84.** At the end it still held what it had bought and not sold, 17 lots net across its products, and
  the portal valued those lots at its settlement price.
- **the score: €110.21,** their sum.

![The score's two parts in each of the Varde rehearsal's three public sessions. Data: `data/sessions.csv`, from
`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/private/portal.py`'s scoring of the uploaded bot.](figures/f03_score_parts.png){#fig-score
fig-alt="Bar chart: in each session, cash and the position's value are hundreds to thousands of euros apart and of opposite sign, and the score, their sum, is between 110 and 137 euros."}

@fig-score shows all three sessions. In sessions 1 and 3 the score is a small difference between two big numbers, in
session 2 between two smaller ones, and in every session one of them, the position's value, depends on a price the portal chooses. Hold that thought: it is why chapter 6 counts the
*mark* among a backtest's assumptions, and why the end of a session matters more than any single tick.

## The idea

### The order book

An exchange is a place where offers to trade wait until someone takes them. Each offer is a *limit order*: buy up to
this many lots at this price or lower, or sell up to this many at this price or higher. The offers waiting at a moment
make up the *order book*: the *bids* (offers to buy) on one side, the *asks* (offers to sell) on the other, each side
grouped into *levels*, one per price (@fig-book).

![One tick of Prosperity 3's Kelp, round 1, day 0. Data: `data/order_book.csv`, from the engine's loader.](figures/f02_order_book.png){#fig-book
fig-alt="An order book: bids of 2 lots at 2,029 and 23 lots at 2,028; asks of 6 lots at 2,030 and 25 lots at 2,032; the mid 2,029.5 and the wall mid 2,030."}

The highest bid is the *best bid* (2,029 here); the lowest ask is the *best ask* (2,030). Together they are the
*touch*, and the gap between them is the *spread*, here 1. Prices move in fixed steps, the *tick size*: 1 credit on
Prosperity, 5 cents on the Varde Exchange. A spread of one tick is as narrow as a book can be.

The plainest single number for "the price" is the *mid*, halfway between the touch:

::: {.eq speak="the mid is the average of the best bid and the best ask"}
$$\text{mid} = \frac{\text{best bid} + \text{best ask}}{2}$$
:::

Here it is 2,029.5. Chapter 3 is about why the mid is often the wrong number to trust, and what the large orders at
2,028 and 2,032, the *walls*, tell you instead.

### Orders and fills

A new order either crosses the book or it doesn't.

- A **buy at or above the best ask** (or a sell at or below the best bid) *crosses*. It trades at once with the
  waiting orders, at their prices, best first. This is *taking*: you pay the spread for trading now.
- An order that **doesn't cross** joins the book and waits. This is *making*, or quoting, and the order is *passive*:
  you offer liquidity and hope someone takes it. When they do, your order is *filled*, at your price.

Among orders at the same price, the earliest is filled first: *price-time priority*. So a waiting order has a place in
a *queue*, and joining a busy level means waiting behind everyone already there.

Exchanges differ in whether a waiting order stays. Prosperity cancels every order at the end of its tick, so a bot
re-quotes each tick; the Varde Exchange lets orders *rest* until filled or cancelled. That one rule changes which
strategies work (chapter 6).

### Position, limits and profit

Your *position* in a product is what you hold: positive after buying more than you sold (*long*), negative after
selling more than you bought (*short*; exchanges in these competitions let you sell what you don't hold). Each product
has a *position limit*, and exchanges enforce it bluntly. On Prosperity, if a tick's orders for a product could take
the position past its limit were they all filled, every one of them is rejected; the Varde Exchange does the same.
A bot that quotes the whole room under its limit on both sides can lose all its orders for a tick by miscounting one.

Profit and loss, *PnL*, is what a bot would have if it closed everything now:

::: {.eq speak="profit is the cash, plus the position times the price it is valued at"}
$$\text{PnL} = \text{cash} + \text{position} \times \text{price}$$
:::

Cash goes down by the price of everything bought and up by everything sold; fees come out of it. The price that
values the position is a choice, which is what the story was about.

### What the data looks like

Every exchange records the same market differently, and the repo meets three shapes:

- **Snapshots** (Prosperity): the book at each tick, a few levels a side, plus a file of the trades between ticks,
  with buyer and seller names when the round reveals them.
- **Prints with an aggressor flag** (the Varde Exchange): each step's book, and each trade marked with which side
  crossed, so you know whether a buyer or a seller was in a hurry.
- **An event log** (LOBSTER, and many real exchanges): every order added, changed, cancelled or executed, from which
  any snapshot can be rebuilt.

Whatever the shape, a *format plug-in* reads it into the engine's one internal form, a `Day` of `Tick`s, each with its
book and its trades. The engine and every tool work on that, never on the exchange's own files (chapter 9). That is
why a new exchange on the day costs a plug-in and an adapter, not a new set of tools.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
The order book is the state, a tick is a time step, and the bot is a policy from state to actions. Two things are less
familiar. The state is partly made of other agents' intentions, which change when you act; a replay freezes them
(chapter 6). And the reward, PnL, is only defined after a choice of price for what you hold, like a metric that needs
a reference you have to pick.
:::
